reference.source: Youmans & Winn Neurological Surgery / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Meningiomas are the most common primary intracranial tumours and are usually slow-growing and benign, arising from the meningeal covering of the brain and spinal cord
Many are asymptomatic and discovered incidentally on imaging performed for other reasons
When symptomatic, features depend on location and result from gradual compression, producing focal deficits, seizures, or symptoms of raised intracranial pressure
They are more common in women and their growth can be influenced by hormonal factors; some carry hormone receptors
On imaging they are typically well-defined, extra-axial, dural-based, avidly and homogeneously enhancing masses, often with a dural tail and sometimes adjacent bony change
Small asymptomatic meningiomas are frequently managed by surveillance imaging, reserving intervention for growth or symptoms
Symptomatic or enlarging tumours are usually treated by surgical resection, with radiotherapy or radiosurgery for residual, recurrent, higher-grade, or surgically inaccessible lesions
Although most are low grade, a minority are atypical or malignant with a greater tendency to recur, so histological grading guides follow-up
reference.pathophysiology: Meningiomas arise from meningothelial (arachnoid cap) cells of the meninges and are therefore extra-axial, growing outside the brain parenchyma and compressing it from the surface. They are typically slow-growing and attached to the dura, and their growth can distort adjacent brain, cranial nerves, and vessels, provoke surrounding oedema, and erode or hyperostose overlying bone. Symptoms arise from mass effect at the specific location rather than infiltration. Most are histologically low grade, but atypical and anaplastic variants show more aggressive behaviour and higher recurrence rates. Prior cranial irradiation and certain genetic conditions increase risk.
additionalInvestigations: MRI brain or spine with contrast to characterise the extra-axial dural-based mass and dural tail
CT to assess associated hyperostosis, calcification, or bony erosion
Serial imaging to monitor growth of incidental or conservatively managed lesions
Histopathology and grading after biopsy or resection
Vascular imaging when preoperative embolisation of a highly vascular tumour is considered
redFlags: Rapid growth or atypical imaging features suggesting a higher-grade tumour
Progressive neurological deficit, new seizures, or cranial nerve compromise
Signs of raised intracranial pressure from a large lesion with oedema and mass effect
Acute deterioration from peritumoural oedema or, rarely, haemorrhage
reference.prognosis: Most meningiomas are benign and, when completely resected, have an excellent prognosis with low recurrence; incompletely removed, atypical, or malignant tumours recur more often and may need adjuvant radiotherapy and closer surveillance.
pitfalls: Assuming every dural-based enhancing mass is a benign meningioma without considering metastasis or other lesions
Over-treating small, stable, asymptomatic incidental tumours
Underestimating the recurrence risk of atypical or malignant subtypes
Overlooking peritumoural oedema as a treatable cause of symptoms
management: Active surveillance with serial contrast MRI for small, asymptomatic, incidentally found tumours
Maximal safe surgical resection as the mainstay for symptomatic or enlarging lesions, aiming for complete removal of tumour and dural attachment
Stereotactic radiosurgery or fractionated radiotherapy for residual, recurrent, atypical or anaplastic tumours and surgically inaccessible sites
Corticosteroids to control symptomatic peritumoural oedema and antiseizure medication for tumour-related seizures
Preoperative embolisation of highly vascular tumours to reduce operative haemorrhage
Histological grading to guide the need for adjuvant radiotherapy and the intensity of follow-up
Neuro-oncology multidisciplinary management with long-term surveillance imaging for recurrence
